item.title: Timing C Code with clock(): A Benchmarking Guide
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
clock() from <time.h> tells us how much CPU time the program has used so far. Call it before and after a piece of code, subtract, and we know how long that code took. We used it in Inline Functions in C to compare a function call with an inlined version, and this post explains how it works and where it can mislead us.

The basics

  • clock() returns a value of type clock_t: the processor time used by the program since it started, in clock ticks.
  • CLOCKS_PER_SEC is the number of ticks per second. Dividing by it converts ticks to seconds.
  • Cast to double before dividing, otherwise integer division throws away the fractions.
#include <stdio.h>
#include <time.h>

int main(void) {
    clock_t start = clock();

    long sum = 0;
    for (long i = 1; i <= 200000000; i++) sum += i % 7;

    clock_t end = clock();
    double seconds = (double)(end - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC;

    printf("sum = %ld\n", sum);
    printf("CLOCKS_PER_SEC = %ld\n", (long)CLOCKS_PER_SEC);
    printf("time = %.3f s\n", seconds);
    return 0;
}
$ gcc -O2 timing.c -o timing && ./timing
sum = 599999998
CLOCKS_PER_SEC = 1000000
time = 0.265 s

On Linux CLOCKS_PER_SEC is 1,000,000 (the POSIX value), so one tick is a microsecond. Do not assume that on other systems; always divide by the constant. The exact times in this post come from one Linux machine with GCC 11.4 and will differ on yours.

Pitfall 1: the optimiser may delete the code we are timing

In the program above we print sum, so the compiler must compute it. If we never use the result, an optimising compiler is allowed to remove the whole loop:

long sum = 0;
for (long i = 1; i <= 200000000; i++) sum += i % 7;   // sum is never used
printf("time = %.3f s\n", (double)(clock() - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC);
$ gcc -O2 dead.c -o dead && ./dead
time = 0.000 s

A loop of 200 million iterations “ran” in zero seconds, because it did not run at all. Built with -O0 the same program reports 0.529 s. So:

Warning

Always use the result of the code being timed (print it, return it, or store it in a volatile variable), so the compiler cannot discard it.

Pitfall 2: one run is noisy

The first run is often slower (cold caches, the CPU still speeding up), and other programs compete for the processor. Run the work several times and report the minimum, which is the run least disturbed by noise:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <time.h>

#define RUNS 5

static long work(void) {
    long sum = 0;
    for (long i = 1; i <= 100000000; i++) sum += i % 7;
    return sum;
}

int main(void) {
    double best = 1e9;
    long result = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < RUNS; r++) {
        clock_t start = clock();
        result = work();
        double t = (double)(clock() - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC;
        printf("run %d: %.3f s\n", r + 1, t);
        if (t < best) best = t;
    }
    printf("result = %ld, best of %d = %.3f s\n", result, RUNS, best);
    return 0;
}
run 1: 0.199 s
run 2: 0.133 s
run 3: 0.133 s
run 4: 0.134 s
run 5: 0.133 s
result = 299999997, best of 5 = 0.133 s

The first run was 50% slower than the rest. Printing result keeps the work from being optimised away (pitfall 1).

Also make the timed work last long enough, ideally at least a few hundredths of a second. A task that finishes in a few microseconds is dominated by the resolution of the clock and the cost of calling clock() itself; wrap it in a loop of many repetitions and divide.

Pitfall 3: CPU time is not wall-clock time

clock() counts time the CPU spent running our program. Time spent waiting (sleeping, reading a file, waiting for the network) is not counted:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main(void) {
    clock_t c0 = clock();
    struct timespec w0, w1;
    clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &w0);

    sleep(1);                                  // waiting, not computing

    clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &w1);
    clock_t c1 = clock();

    printf("clock()         : %.3f s\n", (double)(c1 - c0) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC);
    printf("wall (monotonic): %.3f s\n",
           (w1.tv_sec - w0.tv_sec) + (w1.tv_nsec - w0.tv_nsec) / 1e9);
    return 0;
}
clock()         : 0.000 s
wall (monotonic): 1.000 s

Which one do we want?

We want to know Use
How much computation an algorithm needs clock()
How long the user waits, including I/O and sleeping clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, ...) (POSIX)
Time for a program using several threads wall-clock time; clock() adds up the CPU time of all threads, so it can exceed the elapsed time

A reusable timing helper

Wrapping the pattern in a small function keeps benchmarks tidy:

#include <time.h>

double seconds_since(clock_t start) {
    return (double)(clock() - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC;
}

// usage:
// clock_t t = clock();
// do_work();
// printf("%.3f s\n", seconds_since(t));

Checklist

  1. Compile with the optimisation level you care about (-O2), and compare variants at the same level.
  2. Use the result of the timed code so it is not optimised away.
  3. Repeat and take the minimum (or the median).
  4. Pick CPU time (clock()) or wall time (clock_gettime) on purpose.
  5. Time only the work, not printf or file reading, unless those are what we are measuring.

To compile and run these programs quickly, see Compiling and Running C Programs on Linux.

item.title: Inline Functions in C: When They Help and What Happens Without Them
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
An inline function asks the compiler to insert the function’s body at each call site instead of emitting a jump to a separate piece of code. For tiny functions, the call itself (setting up arguments, jumping, returning) can cost more than the work done inside.

Note

inline is a hint, not a command. The compiler may inline a function without the keyword, or ignore the keyword. The examples below were compiled with GCC 11.4 on Linux; timings will differ on other machines.

Five functions that suit inline

Each is small, called often, and has no loop or recursion of its own. We write them as static inline (the reason is in the last section).

static inline int square(int x) { return x * x; }

static inline int max(int a, int b) { return (a > b) ? a : b; }

static inline int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

static inline void swap(int *m, int *n) {   // called thousands of times in a sort
    int tmp = *m;
    *m = *n;
    *n = tmp;
}

static inline int get_raw_value(const int *ptr) { return *ptr; }   // tiny accessor

What goes wrong when we leave inline out

1. A tiny function in a hot loop

We call the same one-line function 100 million times, once through a normal call and once inlined. To make the comparison fair, __attribute__((noinline)) (a GCC/Clang extension) stops the compiler from quietly inlining the first one for us. The timing uses clock(); see Timing C Code with clock() for how it works and how to avoid misleading numbers.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <time.h>   // clock() and CLOCKS_PER_SEC, explained in the clock() post

#define N 100000000

__attribute__((noinline)) int add_call(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
static inline int add_inline(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

int main(void) {
    clock_t t0 = clock();
    long s1 = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) s1 = add_call(s1, i);
    clock_t t1 = clock();
    long s2 = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) s2 = add_inline(s2, i);
    clock_t t2 = clock();
    printf("call   : sum=%ld  %.3f s\n", s1, (double)(t1 - t0) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC);
    printf("inline : sum=%ld  %.3f s\n", s2, (double)(t2 - t1) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC);
    return 0;
}
$ gcc -O2 inline_bench.c -o inline_bench && ./inline_bench
call   : sum=887459712  0.168 s
inline : sum=887459712  0.067 s

Same answer, about 2.5 times faster inlined. The loop body is so small that the call overhead dominates.

2. A function applied to an array

Inlining also lets the compiler optimise across the call, for example by processing several array elements at once. Here sq_call is kept as a real call and sq_inline is not:

__attribute__((noinline)) int sq_call(int x) { return x * x + 1; }
static inline int sq_inline(int x) { return x * x + 1; }

// ... for each of 20 passes over 10 million ints:
//     b[i] = sq_call(a[i]);     versus     b[i] = sq_inline(a[i]);
call   : 0.368 s
inline : 0.174 s

The real call also blocks the compiler from combining the iterations, so it pays the call cost every time.

3. The function lives in another file

Without link-time optimisation, the compiler compiling main.c cannot see the body of a function defined in add.c. It has no choice but to emit a call, however small the function is. Putting a static inline version in the header fixes that.

/* add.h */
int add(int a, int b);                      /* defined in add.c */
static inline int add_inl(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

/* main.c */
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) s = add(s, i);       /* call into add.c */
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) s = add_inl(s, i);   /* body inlined */

Compile with gcc -O2 -S main.c -o - and look at the assembly: there is one call add@PLT for the first loop and no call at all for add_inl.

4. Don’t judge by an unoptimised build

At -O0, GCC ignores inline. The same benchmark as in example 1:

$ gcc -O0 inline_bench.c -o inline_bench && ./inline_bench
call   : sum=887459712  0.389 s
inline : sum=887459712  0.379 s

No difference. Always compare with -O2.

The counter-case: not every function needs the keyword

Within one file, at -O2, GCC inlines a small function such as add on its own (the assembly for printf("%d", add(2, 3)) contains no call add). The inline keyword matters most for functions in headers, and it should not be added to large functions, because every call site gets its own copy of the body and the executable grows.

Why static inline in headers

In C99 and later, a plain inline function in a header does not provide an external definition. Unless one .c file also contains an extern inline declaration, the linker can fail when the compiler chooses not to inline:

/* h2.h */
inline int twice(int x) { return 2 * x; }
$ gcc -O0 m2.c -o m2
/usr/bin/ld: in function `main': undefined reference to `twice'

(gcc -O2 m2.c happens to work, since the call is inlined, which is exactly why this bug hides until someone builds without optimisation.) Writing static inline gives each file its own private copy, so the header works at every optimisation level and never causes “multiple definition” errors.

Rule of thumb

  • static inline for tiny, hot functions, especially in headers.
  • Leave it off big functions and anything called rarely.
  • Measure with -O2 before believing any speed claim, ours included.

item.title: Recursion in C: sum, factorial and fast power, Step by Step
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Recursion means a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of that problem. Let’s look at a simple example, sum(n), the sum of the first n integers, and trace sum(3) step by step:

GOING DOWN                              RETURNING UP
sum(3) = 3 + sum(2)              ──┐
sum(2) = 2 + sum(1)              ──┤    sum(0) = 0                (base hit)
sum(1) = 1 + sum(0)              ──┤    sum(1) = 1 + 0 = 1
sum(0) = 0   ← base              ──┘    sum(2) = 2 + 1 = 3
                                        sum(3) = 3 + 3 = 6

Each call waits for the one below it, and the additions can only happen on the way back up, once sum(0) has returned.

This is a textbook recursion example. It has the three things every recursive function needs:

  1. A base case that stops the recursion — sum(0) = 0. Without this, it would call sum(-1), sum(-2), … forever (stack overflow).
  2. A recursive case that shrinks the problem — sum(3) calls sum(2), which calls sum(1)… each call gets closer to the base case.
  3. The “unwinding” — once sum(0) returns 0, the answers flow back up: 1+0=1, 2+1=3, 3+3=6.

That “go down, hit bottom, come back up” shape is the heart of all simple recursion. In C, sum looks like this:

#include <stdio.h>

int sum(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;     // BASE CASE
    return n + sum(n - 1);    // RECURSIVE CASE
}

int main(void) {
    printf("%d\n", sum(3));   // 6
    return 0;
}

Another example: factorial, with full step trace

factorial(n) = n × (n-1) × … × 1, and factorial(0) = 1 by definition (the base case).

#include <stdio.h>

long factorial(int n) {
    if (n == 0) {          // BASE CASE: stop here
        return 1;
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1);   // RECURSIVE CASE: shrink n
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i <= 5; i++)
        printf("%d! = %ld\n", i, factorial(i));
    return 0;
}

Compile and run (gcc factorial.c -o factorial && ./factorial; see Compiling and Running C Programs on Linux for faster workflows):

0! = 1
1! = 1
2! = 2
3! = 6
4! = 24
5! = 120

Step-by-step trace of factorial(4)

GOING DOWN                              RETURNING UP
factorial(4) = 4 * factorial(3)  ──┐
factorial(3) = 3 * factorial(2)  ──┤    factorial(0) = 1          (base hit)
factorial(2) = 2 * factorial(1)  ──┤    factorial(1) = 1 * 1 = 1
factorial(1) = 1 * factorial(0)  ──┤    factorial(2) = 2 * 1 = 2
factorial(0) = 1   ← base        ──┘    factorial(3) = 3 * 2 = 6
                                        factorial(4) = 4 * 6 = 24

Notice the multiplication can’t happen until the call below returns ; that’s why the result is computed on the way back up, not on the way down. This is the same shape as the sum example.

Same skeleton, side by side

sum(n) factorial(n)
Base case n == 0 → 0 n == 0 → 1
Recursive case n + sum(n-1) n * factorial(n-1)
How it shrinks n → n-1 n → n-1
Combines results by + *

The only real difference is what operator you apply when coming back up. Recursion’s structure is remarkably reusable — change the base value and the operator, and you get a whole family of functions.

A second example where recursion branches: power

Simple linear recursion calls itself once per step (like sum and factorial). A more interesting form calls itself and combines — here, power computes x^n fast by halving n:

#include <stdio.h>

double power(double x, int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 1.0;                 // BASE: x^0 = 1
    if (n < 0)  return 1.0 / power(x, -n);  // handle negatives
    if (n % 2 == 0) {                       // even n: x^n = (x^(n/2))^2
        double half = power(x, n / 2);
        return half * half;
    }
    return x * power(x, n - 1);             // odd n: peel one off
}

int main(void) {
    printf("%.0f\n", power(2, 10));   // 1024
    printf("%.0f\n", power(3, 4));    // 81
    return 0;
}

Trace of power(2, 10):

power(2,10) → half = power(2,5); return half*half
  power(2,5) → return 2 * power(2,4)
    power(2,4) → half = power(2,2); return half*half
      power(2,2) → half = power(2,1); return half*half
        power(2,1) → return 2 * power(2,0)
          power(2,0) → 1                       (base)
        power(2,1) → 2 * 1 = 2
      power(2,2) → 2 * 2 = 4
    power(2,4) → 4 * 4 = 16
  power(2,5) → 2 * 16 = 32
power(2,10) → 32 * 32 = 1024

This does only ~5 multiplications instead of 10 — the halving is why fast exponentiation is O(log n). Recursion isn’t just elegant; it can be algorithmically better.

How to tell a good recursion example

A good teaching example should:

  • Have an obvious base case you can state in one line (sum(0)=0, 0!=1, x^0=1).
  • Shrink toward the base on every call (n → n-1, n → n/2).
  • Be naturally self-similar — the problem really is “a smaller copy of itself.”
  • Show the returning-up phase clearly (the sum trace does this well).

The sum example hits all four, so it is a good one to teach first.

The pitfalls to mention alongside it

Pitfall Symptom
No base case, or one never reached Infinite recursion → stack overflow / segfault
Wrong base value Off-by-one results (e.g. sum base 1 instead of 0)
Not shrinking (e.g. calls sum(n) again) Infinite recursion
Deep recursion (n = 1,000,000) Stack overflow even when logically correct
Redundant recomputation (naive Fibonacci) Exponential blowup — fib(40) takes seconds

The one-line rule

Recursion = base case + smaller subproblem + combine on the way back up. If you can write those three lines, you’ve written the function.

The sum example has all three parts, which makes it a good first example. factorial is the natural next one because it’s the same skeleton with a different operator, and power shows that recursion can also branch and be faster than a loop.

Tip

The same ideas carry over to other languages. See Recursion in R: Functions That Call Themselves for base and recursive cases, Recall(), recursion on nested lists and R’s depth limits.

item.title: Stack Overflow Explained, with Examples from C, R and Python
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
This post follows Recursion in C and Recursion in R: what happens when recursion goes too deep, and what to do about it.

What a stack overflow actually is

Every function call pushes a stack frame onto the call stack, a block of memory holding that call’s parameters, local variables, and return address. The stack is a fixed-size region decided when the program starts (typically 8 MB for the main thread on Linux and 1 MB on Windows).

   high address
   ┌──────────────┐
   │  frame main  │
   ├──────────────┤
   │  frame f(3)  │  ← each recursive call pushes another frame
   ├──────────────┤
   │  frame f(2)  │
   ├──────────────┤
   │  frame f(1)  │
   ├──────────────┤
   │     ...      │  ← keep pushing → grow downward
   └──────────────┘
   low address         ← the stack limit is here

When frames keep piling up past that limit, the program writes off the end of the stack: a stack overflow. What happens next depends on the language’s runtime:

Language On overflow Catchable?
C Segfault (SIGSEGV) — process dies ❌ No
R Error: evaluation nested too deeply (or node stack overflow when expressions is raised) ✅ Yes (an R error)
R (C stack exhausted) Error: C stack usage … is too close to the limit, can crash ⚠️ Sometimes
Python RecursionError ✅ Yes (a Python exception)

The cause is always one of two things: 1. No base case, or a base case never reached → infinite recursion. 2. A correct but very deep recursion (depth ~10⁵–10⁶) → legitimate algorithm, too many frames.

C: dies with a segfault

Infinite recursion (no base case)

#include <stdio.h>

int sum(int n) {
    return n + sum(n - 1);   // ❌ never stops
}

int main(void) {
    printf("%d\n", sum(3));
    return 0;
}
$ gcc so1.c -o so1 && ./so1
Segmentation fault (core dumped)

Each call pushes a frame; after a few hundred thousand frames (depending on frame size and stack limit), the stack runs out and the CPU faults on the write. There is no error message and no recovery; the process is just gone.

Warning

With optimisation the result can differ. Compiled with gcc -O2, this same program did not crash on our machine: it ran forever, because the compiler turned the tail call into a loop. A runaway recursion is a bug either way, but do not count on a segfault to reveal it.

A “correct” recursion that’s still too deep

int sum_to(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;          // ✅ proper base case
    return n + sum_to(n - 1);
}
// sum_to(10000000);  → segfault at -O0

The base case is fine, but depth = n frames. At 10⁷ calls × a few dozen bytes per frame, that is hundreds of MB of stack, far past the 8 MB limit. We compiled it with plain gcc and it segfaulted.

Note

With gcc -O2 the same program ran without crashing, because GCC rewrote the recursion as a loop. (It printed -2004260032, since the true sum overflows int; use long for real work.) The C standard does not promise this optimisation, so the code is still unsafe.

The sneakier version: huge local arrays

void recurse(int n) {
    int buffer[100000];            // ~400 KB per frame!
    recurse(n + 1);
}

About 20 calls are enough to fill an 8 MB stack, because each frame carries a 400 KB local array. This is why frame size matters as much as depth. (We ran a version that recurses 1000 levels; it segfaulted.)

Inspect your limits:

ulimit -s              # stack size in KB (e.g. 8192 = 8 MB)
gcc -fstack-usage ...  # per-function frame sizes in a .su file

R: usually an R error, sometimes a C-stack crash

Infinite recursion → R’s expressions limit

f <- function(n) n + f(n - 1)
f(1)
Error: evaluation nested too deeply: infinite recursion / options(expressions=)?

R doesn’t let nesting run away silently: it counts nested expressions and stops at options(expressions), which defaults to 5000. This is a catchable R error (you can wrap it in tryCatch), not a process crash.

A legitimate deep recursion that still fails

sum_to <- function(n) if (n == 0) 0 else n + sum_to(n - 1)

sum_to(100)     # fine
sum_to(10000)   # Error: evaluation nested too deeply

You can raise the limit:

options(expressions = 100000)
sum_to(10000)    # works
sum_to(100000)   # Error: node stack overflow

R 4.6 stopped the second call with node stack overflow, R’s own evaluation stack. Other builds, or functions with larger frames, can instead hit the C stack and report:

Error: C stack usage  7970000 is too close to the limit

That is the actual OS stack filling, closer to C’s situation. Raising expressions does not grow the stack; it only moves the point where R complains.

Inspect it:

getOption("expressions")   # 5000 by default
options(expressions = 20000)

Python: a clean, catchable RecursionError

Infinite recursion

def sum_to(n):
    return n + sum_to(n - 1)     # no base case

sum_to(3)
RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded

Python counts Python frames and stops at sys.getrecursionlimit() — default 1000. Unlike C, this is a normal exception you can catch:

try:
    sum_to(3)
except RecursionError:
    print("too deep!")

The trap: raising the limit can segfault

import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(1000000)   # ⚠️ dangerous
sum_to(1000000)                  # segfault, not RecursionError

setrecursionlimit only raises Python’s counter. The C stack behind it is still ~8 MB. If CPython’s own C-level recursion runs out before the Python counter trips, you get a hard segfault, with no exception and no message. On Python 3.10 this exact example dumped core on our machine. (Recent CPython versions add C-stack guards that convert some of these to RecursionError, but it is not safe to rely on.)

A correct deep recursion that still fails

def sum_to(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    return n + sum_to(n - 1)

sum_to(100)     # ✅ 5050
sum_to(10000)   # ❌ RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded in comparison

How to avoid it, in any language

1. Always have a reachable base case that shrinks the problem

int sum(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;   // base case
    return n + sum(n - 1);  // shrinks toward base
}

If the argument doesn’t move toward the base on every call, it’s infinite.

2. Convert linear recursion to a loop (the best fix when you can)

This is the real solution for sum, factorial, and any “n → n−1” chain. Depth O(n) becomes depth O(1):

// C
long sum_to(int n) {
    long s = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) s += i;
    return s;
}
# Python
def sum_to(n):
    return sum(range(n + 1))     # or a loop
# R
sum_to <- function(n) sum(seq_len(n))

No stack growth at all — the loop lives in one frame.

3. Use an explicit stack (manual recursion)

For trees/graphs where recursion is natural, keep your own stack on the heap, which is much larger than the call stack:

def dfs(root):
    stack = [root]
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        visit(node)
        stack.extend(node.children)   # no call frames, no depth limit
// C — same idea
void dfs(Node *root) {
    Node *stack[1000];
    int top = 0;
    stack[top++] = root;
    while (top > 0) {
        Node *n = stack[--top];
        visit(n);
        for (int i = 0; i < n->nchild; i++)
            stack[top++] = n->child[i];
    }
}

4. Halve the problem instead of decrementing it

The power example from the C recursion post is the template. n → n−1 gives depth n; n → n/2 gives depth log₂ n — a million-step problem becomes ~20 frames:

def power(x, n):
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    half = power(x, n // 2)     # depth = log2(n), not n
    return half * half if n % 2 == 0 else x * half * half

power(2, 1000000) recurses about 20 levels (we ran it in Python without trouble). sum_to(1000000) with n-1 would need a million.

5. Memoisation: fixes redundant recursion, not deep recursion

Naive Fibonacci is O(2ⁿ) calls but only depth n. Memoizing cuts the number of calls dramatically, but does not reduce depth — fib(10000) still recurses 10,000 levels. Use it for speed, not for stack safety.

6. Trampoline: portable “fake tail recursion”

C, R, and Python do not guarantee tail-call optimization (TCO). So return f(x) still pushes a frame. A trampoline turns recursion into a loop:

def trampoline(f, *args):
    result = f(*args)
    while callable(result):
        result = result()
    return result

def sum_to(n, acc=0):
    if n == 0:
        return acc
    return lambda: sum_to(n - 1, acc + n)   # return a thunk, don't call

print(trampoline(sum_to, 1000000))          # 500000500000, no RecursionError

Each “recursive” step returns a thunk and the loop calls it, so only one frame is ever live. This is how you do deep recursion in Python without touching the limit.

7. Last resort: increase the stack (a band-aid, not a fix)

ulimit -s 65536        # Linux: 64 MB stack for this shell/process
import threading
threading.stack_size(64 * 1024 * 1024)   # Python: run in a big-stack thread
# no clean per-script control of the C stack: rewrite the function instead

This buys headroom but doesn’t remove the bug — a truly infinite recursion still overflows, just later. Treat it as a stopgap while you rewrite.

Summary: what to do

Situation Fix
No base case / never reached Add one; ensure the argument moves toward it
Simple linear recursion (n-1 chain) Rewrite as a loop — depth O(1)
Tree/graph traversal Explicit stack on the heap
Divide-and-conquer Ensure it halves (depth log n)
Deep recursion, can’t rewrite easily Trampoline (portable; no TCO in C/R/Python)
Need more headroom temporarily Raise stack (ulimit -s, thread stack size) — stopgap
Just need speed Memoise, but it will not fix depth

The one-line rule: recursion depth is a resource like memory, and O(n) depth is a bomb for large n. Prefer iteration (O(1) depth), halving (O(log n) depth), or an explicit heap stack whenever the input can be large. Languages differ in how loudly they fail (C segfaults, Python and R raise catchable errors), but none of them will save us from a bad recursion design.

item.title: The Dots Argument (…) in R Functions
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
In R, ... (dot-dot-dot, also called the ellipsis or dots argument) is a special parameter that lets a function accept any number of extra arguments. It has two main uses:

  1. passing arguments on to another function, and
  2. collecting a variable-length set of inputs, as c(), paste() and list() do.

Use 1: Passing arguments to an inner function

A wrapper can fix some settings and let the caller customise everything else, without listing every possible argument.

# Force the colour and symbol, but let the user set titles, labels, axes, ...
my_plot <- function(x, y, ...) {
  plot(x, y, col = "royalblue", pch = 16, ...)
}

# main and xlab are not named in my_plot(), yet they reach plot()
my_plot(1:10, 1:10, main = "My Custom Chart", xlab = "X Axis Index")

Use 2: Collecting inputs with list(...)

To use the extra arguments inside the function, convert ... into an ordinary list.

summarize_inputs <- function(...) {
  input_list <- list(...)
  cat("We received", length(input_list), "arguments.\n")
  print(names(input_list))
  invisible(input_list)
}

res <- summarize_inputs(a = 10, b = "hello", c = TRUE)
We received 3 arguments.
[1] "a" "b" "c"

Two related helpers are worth knowing: ...length() gives the number of arguments, and ..1, ..2, … pick them by position.

Where does ... go?

At the end: fixed inputs first, extras last

Put ... last when the function has required inputs and ... only catches optional settings for a downstream call.

my_plot <- function(x, y, ...) {
  plot(x, y, ...)
}

# 1:10 goes to x, 1:10 to y, and col travels down through ...
my_plot(1:10, 1:10, col = "red")

At the beginning: collect data first

Put ... first when the function’s job is to gather an unknown number of objects (like c() or paste()). Every argument after ... must then be named in the call, because R never matches them by position.

f <- function(..., named_arg = "default") {
  list(n = length(list(...)), named_arg = named_arg)
}

str(f(1, 2, 3, "custom_value"))                       # swallowed by ...
str(f(1, 2, 3, named_arg = "custom_value"))           # as intended
List of 2
 $ n        : int 4
 $ named_arg: chr "default"
List of 2
 $ n        : int 3
 $ named_arg: chr "custom_value"

In the first call "custom_value" is counted as a fourth data input and named_arg keeps its default.

Combining both uses

A single ... can only do one job. If it collects the data, the styling arguments end up in the data too. In the example below, passing col and border through list(...) makes mean() fail on them. So we take the data as an explicit argument and keep ... for the plot settings.

analyze_and_plot <- function(data_list, plot_title = "Data Analysis", ...) {
  means <- sapply(data_list, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  cat("Calculated means for", length(data_list), "groups:\n")
  print(means)

  # col, border, las, ... go straight to boxplot()
  boxplot(data_list, main = plot_title, ...)
  invisible(means)
}

groups <- list(
  A = c(10, 12, 15, 14, 18),
  B = c(22, 25, 28, 21, 24),
  C = c(5, 7, 8, 6, 9)
)

analyze_and_plot(
  groups,
  plot_title = "Experimental Results",
  col = c("tomato", "gold", "deepskyblue"),
  border = "darkgray"
)
Calculated means for 3 groups:
   A    B    C
13.8 24.0  7.0
WarningPitfalls
  • Misspelt arguments pass silently through .... plot(1:3, 1:3, colr = "red") raises no error. R only warns that "colr" is not a graphical parameter, and the colour is ignored, so check the warnings.
  • One ... cannot serve two purposes. Decide whether it holds data or settings. Use list(...) for the first, and an explicit argument plus ... for the second.
  • Arguments after ... need their full name. Partial matching does not apply to them.

Key takeaways

  • list(...) turns the extra arguments into a list you can count, name-check or loop over.
  • Passing ... to another function forwards settings without the wrapper knowing they exist.
  • Put ... last for optional pass-through settings, and first for collecting data, remembering that anything after it must be named.

Reference

  • DataFlair, R Arguments Introduction

item.title: Fish vs Bash Syntax: A Practical Cheat Sheet
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Bash is the default shell on most Linux systems and follows the POSIX conventions that countless scripts rely on. Fish (the Friendly Interactive SHell) deliberately breaks from them to get a cleaner syntax and a better interactive experience. It is not POSIX-compliant, so Bash habits do not always carry over.

The examples below were run in fish 3.3 and Bash 5. They are the differences we meet most often.

Syntax at a glance

Feature Bash Fish
POSIX compliant Yes No
Set a variable NAME=value (no spaces around =) set NAME value
Export a variable export NAME=value set -gx NAME value
Local variable local name=value (in a function) set -l name value
Command substitution `cmd` or $(cmd) (cmd)
For loop for f in *.txt; do echo "$f"; done for f in *.txt; echo $f; end
While loop while cond; do ...; done while cond; ...; end
Condition if [ -f file.txt ]; then ...; fi if test -f file.txt; ...; end
Last exit code $? $status
Arguments $1, $@, $# $argv[1], $argv, (count $argv)
Arrays arr=(one two); echo ${arr[0]} set arr one two; echo $arr[1]
Strings ${foo%bar}, ${foo#bar}, ${foo/bar/baz} the string builtin
Arithmetic $((2 + 3)) math 2 + 3
Function greet() { echo "Hi $1"; } function greet; echo "Hi $argv[1]"; end
Alias alias gs='git status' abbr -a gs 'git status' (or alias)

The main pattern: Bash closes blocks with fi, done and esac, and fish closes every block with end.

Variables

# Bash
name="Ada Lovelace"
export EDITOR=vim
# fish
set name "Ada Lovelace"
set -gx EDITOR vim

The set flags control scope: -l local to the block or function, -g global to the session, -x exported to child processes, -U universal (shared by all fish sessions and remembered across restarts). Remove a variable with set -e name.

Fish does not split variables on whitespace, so the quoting habit "$file" is mostly unnecessary. A file called my pic.jpg stored in $f is passed as one argument:

set f "my pic.jpg"
mv $f renamed.jpg      # works, no quotes needed

Command substitution

files=$(ls | wc -l)
set files (ls | wc -l)

In fish the output is split on newlines only, so a command that prints three lines gives a list of three items:

set lines (printf 'x y\nz\n')
count $lines           # 2

Conditions and tests

if [ -f file.txt ]; then
    echo "found"
elif [ -d file.txt ]; then
    echo "a folder"
else
    echo "missing"
fi
if test -f file.txt
    echo "found"
else if test -d file.txt
    echo "a folder"
else
    echo "missing"
end

Fish has no [ ... ] or [[ ... ]] syntax. It uses the test command, which also accepts -gt, -lt, -eq and string comparisons with =.

Chaining works with && and || in recent fish versions, and fish also has the words and, or and not:

mkdir build; and cd build
make; or echo "build failed"

The exit code of the last command is $status, not $?:

false
echo $status           # 1

Switch statements

case "$animal" in
    c*) echo "starts with c" ;;
    *)  echo "other" ;;
esac
switch $animal
    case 'c*'
        echo "starts with c"
    case '*'
        echo "other"
end

Fish does not fall through and needs no ;;.

Loops

for i in $(seq 1 3); do echo $i; done
for ((i = 0; i < 3; i++)); do echo $i; done
for i in (seq 1 3); echo $i; end

Fish has no C-style for ((...)) loop, so use seq (or while with math). A countdown:

set n 3
while test $n -gt 0
    echo $n
    set n (math $n - 1)
end

Arrays

Every fish variable is a list. Indexing starts at 1, negative indices count from the end, and ranges are supported:

set arr one two three
echo $arr[1]           # one
echo $arr[-1]          # three
echo $arr[2..3]        # two three
count $arr             # 3
set -a arr four        # append
arr=(one two three)
echo ${arr[0]}         # one (Bash indexes from 0)
echo ${arr[-1]}        # three
echo ${#arr[@]}        # 3

Strings

Bash uses parameter-expansion tricks like ${f%.txt}. Fish has a single string command with sub-commands, which is easier to read and remember:

Task Bash Fish
Remove extension ${f%.*} string replace -r '\.[^.]*$' '' $f
Replace all ${f//a/b} string replace -a a b $f
Lowercase / uppercase ${f,,} / ${f^^} string lower $f / string upper $f
Length ${#f} string length $f
Substring ${f:0:6} string sub -s 1 -l 6 $f
Split IFS=. read -ra p <<< "$f" string split . $f
Regex match [[ $s =~ [0-9]+ ]] string match -r '\d+' $s

For example, string split . report.final.txt prints report, final and txt on separate lines.

Arithmetic

echo $((2 + 3 * 4))    # 14
echo (math 2 + 3 '*' 4)   # 14
echo (math 7 / 2)         # 3.5

Quote * in math, otherwise fish treats it as a wildcard. Unlike Bash’s integer-only $((...)), math returns decimals.

Functions

greet() {
    echo "Hi, $1"
}
function greet
    echo "Hi, $argv[1]"
end

To keep a fish function for later sessions, run funcsave greet. It writes ~/.config/fish/functions/greet.fish. Use functions greet to view a function’s code.

Other behaviours that surprise Bash users

  • No match is an error. In Bash, an unmatched *.xyz stays as the literal text. Fish stops with No matches for wildcard, which prevents a command from running on a name that does not exist.
  • Redirections. 2>&1 and &> work as in Bash. Heredocs (<<EOF) and process substitution with <(cmd) are different or missing: fish uses psub (diff (sort a | psub) (sort b | psub)), and for multiline input we pipe printf or echo.
  • Config file. Bash reads ~/.bashrc. Fish reads ~/.config/fish/config.fish. Add to the path with fish_add_path ~/bin instead of editing PATH by hand.
  • Abbreviations vs aliases. abbr expands to the full command as we type, so history and the screen show what really ran. alias in fish is just a small function.
  • Interactive extras. Syntax highlighting, history-based autosuggestions (accept with →) and tab completions from man pages are on by default. fish_config opens a web page for choosing themes and prompts.
  • Portability. Bash scripts run nearly everywhere. Fish scripts need fish installed and break if Bash runs them.

Scripts: keep Bash for portable ones

Put the interpreter on the first line so that each script runs under the shell it was written for, whichever shell we type it in:

#!/usr/bin/env bash      # portable script
#!/usr/bin/env fish      # fish script

A common setup is to use fish interactively and write shared or server scripts in Bash. We can still run a one-off Bash command from fish with bash -c 'echo $((2+3))'.

Using Bash tools from fish

Some tools (for example nvm, conda or Python’s venv activation) ship Bash-only setup scripts. Look for a fish version first (activate.fish for virtual environments), a fish plugin, or a helper such as bass, which runs a Bash script and copies the resulting variables into fish.

Summary

  • Use set instead of NAME=value, and end instead of fi/done/esac.
  • Variables are lists, indexed from 1, and are not word-split.
  • Use string and math instead of ${...} and $((...)).
  • Use $status and $argv instead of $? and $1.
  • Keep portable scripts in Bash and use fish for daily interactive work.

References

  • Fish for bash users (fish documentation)
  • Bash vs Zsh vs Fish (Tecmint)

item.title: git mv vs. mv: Renaming and Deleting Files in a Git Repository
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
The difference between git mv and plain mv is small but worth knowing. git mv moves the file and stages the change in one step. mv only changes the disk, so we have to tell Git what happened. The same goes for git rm and rm.

Git does not store renames as a special action. It stores snapshots, and when we run git status or git log it detects that a deleted file and a new file have the same content, and labels the pair a rename. That is why both routes below end in the same place.

Moving or renaming

Plain commands Git commands
Move or rename mv old.js new.js git mv old.js new.js
What Git sees old.js deleted, new.js untracked rename, already staged
Extra steps git rm old.js and git add new.js none

With git mv

git mv old_name.js new_name.js
git status --short
R  old_name.js -> new_name.js

The rename is staged and ready to commit.

With plain mv

mv old_name.js new_name.js
git status --short
 D old_name.js
?? new_name.js

Git sees a deleted file and an untracked file. Staging only the new one is a common mistake:

git add new_name.js
git status --short
A  new_name.js
 D old_name.js

The deletion is still unstaged, so a commit now would contain the new file but leave the old one in the repository. We need to stage both:

git rm old_name.js     # stages the deletion (the file is already gone from disk)
git add new_name.js

or, in one step:

git add -A
R  old_name.js -> new_name.js

git add -A is also the easy way to stage a whole batch of manual moves, or renames done in a file manager or editor such as VS Code.

Note

git mv only works on files Git already tracks. For an untracked file it stops with fatal: not under version control, so use plain mv there.

Deleting

Plain command Git command
Delete a file rm file.txt git rm file.txt
What Git sees deleted, not staged deleted, staged 
rm file.txt
git status --short       #  D file.txt   (not staged)

git rm file.txt
git status --short       # D  file.txt   (staged)

git rm also works after the file has already been removed by hand, as above: it just stages the deletion.

Stop tracking a file but keep it on disk

If we committed a file by mistake, such as a .env with secrets, we want Git to forget it without deleting our copy:

git rm --cached .env
git status --short
D  .env
?? .env

The file stays on disk, but Git now lists it as untracked. To keep it from being added again, put it in .gitignore.

Warning

git rm --cached removes the file from future commits only. It stays in the repository’s history, so a secret that was committed should be treated as exposed and changed.

Rename history

After a rename, git log --follow lists the commits from before the rename too:

git log --follow --oneline new_name.js

Without --follow, the log of the new name starts at the rename.

Summary

  • git mv = mv + staging. Plain mv plus git add -A gives the same result.
  • git rm = rm + staging.
  • git rm --cached stops tracking and keeps the file.
  • Git detects renames from the content, so both routes give the same commit.

item.title: How Statistics Powers Machine Learning, AI and Robotics
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Statistics is the quiet engine of machine learning, artificial intelligence and robotics. It hides beneath layers of code and hardware, yet it sits behind every prediction, decision and action: from a simple linear regression to a deep neural network, from a robot crossing a cluttered room to a language model writing a paragraph. Statistics gives these systems a way to learn from data, measure uncertainty and choose well.

In this post we look at where statistics sits in each field, and why skipping it means building on sand.

Statistics: The Language of Learning from Data

Machine learning is about finding patterns in data. But data are noisy, incomplete and variable, and statistics supplies the tools to describe that noise, model the signal underneath and predict with a stated level of confidence.

  • Probability distributions model how likely each outcome is.
  • Estimation theory infers parameters from samples.
  • Hypothesis testing decides whether a pattern is real or just chance.
  • Bayesian inference updates our beliefs as new data arrive.

Without these, a model is little more than a guess.

Machine Learning: Statistics in Modern Clothing

Many ML algorithms are classical statistical methods under a new name.

ML method Statistical view
Linear regression A model for a continuous outcome
Logistic regression A classifier built on the logistic function
Decision trees Recursive partitioning, a non-parametric technique
Support vector machines Maximum-margin classifiers from statistical learning theory
Neural networks Nonlinear regression, usually trained by maximum likelihood

The same holds for the core ideas. The bias-variance tradeoff, the curse of dimensionality and cross-validation are statistical concepts. Measuring generalisation error is statistics. L1 and L2 regularisation act as statistical priors on the parameters, and dropout can be read as an approximation to Bayesian model averaging.

Deep learning is no exception. Stochastic gradient descent is a statistical optimisation method, batch normalisation is a statistical stabilisation trick, and probabilistic deep learning combines neural networks with Bayesian inference.

Artificial Intelligence: Reasoning Under Uncertainty

AI is broader than ML: it is about agents that reason, plan and act. The real world is uncertain, and statistics is the calculus of that uncertainty.

  • Bayesian networks represent probabilistic relationships between variables.
  • Hidden Markov models drive speech recognition and part-of-speech tagging.
  • Markov decision processes (MDPs) and their partially observable version (POMDPs) are the foundation of reinforcement learning, where an agent maximises reward in a stochastic environment.
  • Natural language processing relies on statistical language models, from n-grams to Transformers. Even the largest LLMs are trained by maximum likelihood on huge text corpora.

AI without statistics is a philosopher without logic: full of ideas, with no rigorous way to test them.

Robotics: Where Statistics Meets the Physical World

Robots face sensor noise, imperfect actuators and changing surroundings. For them statistics is not optional; it decides whether a task succeeds or fails.

  • State estimation: Kalman filters, extended Kalman filters and particle filters estimate a robot’s position, velocity and orientation from noisy sensor readings.
  • Sensor fusion: combining cameras, LiDAR, IMUs and GPS needs probabilistic models that weigh how reliable each source is.
  • SLAM (simultaneous localisation and mapping): a textbook statistical problem, since both the map and the robot’s own position are uncertain.
  • Control under uncertainty: stochastic control, such as linear-quadratic-Gaussian (LQG) control, models the noise explicitly and minimises expected cost.
  • Planning under uncertainty: POMDPs handle navigation and manipulation when the state is not fully observable.

The book Probabilistic Robotics by Thrun, Burgard and Fox is, in effect, a statistics text for roboticists.

The Common Thread: From Data to Decisions

ML, AI and robotics all involve decisions under uncertainty, and statistics supplies each piece:

Need Statistical tool
Represent uncertainty Probability distributions
Learn from data Estimation and inference
Judge performance Likelihood, risk, expected loss
Choose the best action Bayesian decision theory, utility maximisation

Whether we classify an email as spam, predict the next word or steer a self-driving car, we are solving a statistical problem.

The Future: Statistics Keeps Driving Progress

As AI systems grow more complex, the need for statistical rigour grows with them. Causal inference moves AI beyond correlation towards causation. Uncertainty quantification is critical for safe autonomous systems. Probabilistic programming makes statistical models easier to build and deploy at scale.

The next breakthroughs in ML, AI and robotics will come from embracing statistics more deeply, not from ignoring it.

Summary

Statistics is how these fields learn from data, reason under uncertainty and act in a noisy world. To build truly intelligent systems we must do more than respect it; we must master it, because at the heart of every smart algorithm is a statistical heartbeat.

item.title: How to Charge a Laptop Battery Properly: The 20–80% Rule
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Modern laptops and phones use lithium-ion batteries, and they age according to how we charge them. The short version: keep the charge between roughly 20% and 80%, and avoid heat.

Should we charge at 20%?

Yes. Plugging in around 20% is a good habit. Letting the battery drain to 0% puts stress on the cells and wears them faster, so we should not wait until the laptop dies.

Why the 20–80% range works

  • Avoid deep discharges. Running to empty is hard on the battery chemistry.
  • Avoid sitting at 100%. A full battery is held at high voltage, which also speeds up wear, especially when it is warm.
  • Longer life. Staying in the middle of the range is commonly reported to give many more charge cycles than going 0–100% every time. The exact numbers vary by battery, so treat any specific figure with caution.

Is it fine to charge at 40% or 60%?

Absolutely. Lithium-ion batteries are under the least stress near the middle of their range, and a top-up from 40% to 80% is only a partial cycle, which is gentler than a deep discharge.

There is no “memory effect” in lithium-ion cells (that was an old nickel-cadmium problem), so we never need to drain the battery before charging, and we do not need to calibrate it every month. We can top up whenever it is convenient.

Best practices

  1. Recharge around 20%, before the laptop drops into single digits.
  2. Use a charge limiter if the laptop mostly stays plugged in at a desk. Most makers provide one that caps the charge at about 80%:
    • ASUS: Battery Health Charging
    • Lenovo: Conservation Mode
    • Dell: Dell Power Manager
    • macOS: Optimized Battery Charging
  3. Watch the heat. Gaming or video editing makes the laptop hot, and a hot, fully charged battery ages fastest. Keep the vents clear and avoid charging on a bed or sofa.
Tip

Staying plugged in is fine as long as a limit is set. Without one, the battery sits at 100% all day, which is the habit we want to avoid.

The same rules apply to phones

Phones use the same lithium-ion technology, so everything above carries over: short, frequent top-ups are easier on the battery than long sessions, we should avoid dropping below 20%, and we should avoid leaving the phone at 100% for hours overnight.

Both major platforms can manage this automatically:

  • iPhone: Settings → Battery → Battery Health & Charging. Turn on Optimized Battery Charging, or on iPhone 15 and newer set an 80% Limit.
  • Android: Look for Protect Battery or Adaptive Charging in the battery settings (Samsung, Pixel, OnePlus and others). It caps the charge at about 80% or slows charging overnight.

Summary

Do Avoid
Charge between 20% and 80% Draining to 0%
Top up whenever convenient Sitting at 100% for hours
Enable the built-in charge limit Charging a hot laptop under heavy load

References

  • Student laptop battery health (Chargie)
  • Should I leave my laptop plugged in all the time? (How-To Geek)
  • Battery 20-80 rule (SmartAction)

item.title: Adding giscus Comments to a Quarto Blog
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
giscus is an open-source, ad-free comment system that stores every comment as a GitHub Discussion. Readers sign in with GitHub, and we get moderation, notifications and email replies without running a server. Quarto supports giscus natively, so the whole setup is a few GitHub settings plus one block of YAML.

Step 1: Prepare the GitHub repository

The comments live in a repository, so we prepare it first.

  1. Make the repository public. giscus does not work with a private repository.
  2. Enable Discussions. On the repository page, open Settings, scroll to Features and tick Discussions.
  3. Install the giscus app. Open the giscus app page, click Install, and give it access to the chosen repository.
  4. Get the IDs. On giscus.app, type username/repo-name in the Repository box and choose a discussion Category (for example General). Keep the page open: further down it prints a <script> block with the values data-repo-id and data-category-id. We need both in the next step.
Tip

Choose the category General (or a dedicated one) rather than Announcements. Announcements is meant for posts from maintainers, so it can limit who may start a discussion.

Step 2: Add the configuration

giscus gives us HTML, but Quarto writes the script tag for us. We only translate each data-* attribute into a YAML key: data-repo-id becomes repo-id, data-category-id becomes category-id, and so on.

The block goes under the website: key in _quarto.yml when we want comments on every page:

website:
  comments:
    giscus:
      repo: username/repo-name
      repo-id: "R_kgDOxxxxxxx"          # from giscus.app
      category: "General"
      category-id: "DIC_kwDOxxxxxxx"    # from giscus.app
      mapping: pathname                 # how a page is matched to a discussion
      reactions-enabled: true           # emoji reactions
      input-position: bottom            # comment box below the comments
      loading: lazy                     # load only when scrolled into view

The mapping option decides how a page finds its discussion. pathname and url are the common choices: each page gets one discussion, created the first time someone comments.

Warning

Changing mapping later, or moving a post to a new address, starts a new, empty discussion for it. Choose once and keep the URLs stable.

Step 3: Comments on posts only

A blog usually wants comments under the posts, but not on the About page or the homepage. For that, keep the block out of _quarto.yml and put it in posts/_metadata.yml instead. Every file in that folder inherits it.

In a _metadata.yml file the options are top-level keys, so there is no website: line:

# posts/_metadata.yml
comments:
  giscus:
    repo: username/repo-name
    repo-id: "R_kgDOxxxxxxx"
    category: "General"
    category-id: "DIC_kwDOxxxxxxx"
    mapping: url
    reactions-enabled: true
    input-position: bottom
    language: en

Then render. A single post is enough to test it:

quarto render posts/my-post.qmd

Posts that were rendered earlier only get the comment box when they are rendered again, so after the first setup it is worth running a full quarto render.

Hiding comments on one page

Even inside the folder, a single page can opt out through its front matter:

---
title: "A post without comments"
comments: false
---

Theme

If the site has a light and a dark theme, we can leave theme out. Quarto then follows the reader’s choice from the theme toggle. To force one look instead, set theme: light, theme: dark or theme: preferred_color_scheme (follow the operating system) under giscus:.

Troubleshooting

  • The box says “giscus is not installed on this repository”: install the app (step 1.3) for that exact repository.
  • No box appears at all: check that the block sits in the right file (website: for _quarto.yml, top level for _metadata.yml) and that the page was re-rendered.
  • “Discussion not found” appears and never changes: the discussion is only created when the first comment is posted, so this is normal for a new page.

Reference

  • Quarto: website comments, for every option of the comments key.
  • giscus.app, for the configuration page that generates the IDs.

item.title: What Is Git? A Plain-English Explanation
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Think of Git as an “Undo” button and a time machine for a folder of files, combined with a way for several people to work on the same project without stepping on each other’s toes.

We do not need to know how to code to understand it. Let’s imagine we are writing a book with a few friends.

The old way, without Git

We write Chapter 1. A friend wants to add a paragraph, so we email them the file. They edit it and send it back. Soon the folder holds:

  • Book_v1.docx
  • Book_v2_final.docx
  • Book_final_ACTUAL_final.docx

If someone makes a mistake, we dig through old copies to find the good version. If two people edit the same page at once, merging their work by hand is a nightmare.

The Git way

Instead of passing copies of the whole book around, Git acts as a record keeper for the project. Four ideas cover most of it.

1. Commit: a save point

A commit is a snapshot of the project at one moment, saved together with a short note.

  • We write a paragraph and commit it with the note “Added a paragraph about dragons.”
  • We fix a typo and commit again: “Fixed a typo in Chapter 1.”

The result is a timeline of every change, who made it, when, and why. If we break something, we can go back to any earlier point.

2. Branch: a parallel universe

Suppose we want to kill off a character in Chapter 5, but a co-author wants to keep them alive. Instead of arguing, each of us creates a branch. We make our changes in our own universe, and the original book stays untouched until we decide otherwise.

3. Merge: bringing the work together

When both of us are done, we merge the branches back into the main timeline. Git compares the versions and combines the changes automatically. If we both edited the same sentence in different ways, Git does not guess. It flags a conflict and asks us to choose which version to keep, so nobody’s work is silently deleted.

4. Repository: the project and its memory

A repository (or repo) is the project folder together with its whole history. It can live on our computer, and a copy can live on a hosting site such as GitHub, which is how friends share and sync their work.

What it looks like in practice

We said no code was needed, but here is the same story as real commands, in a new folder. We ran them to produce the output shown.

git init                                  # start a repository
echo "Chapter 1" > book.txt
git add book.txt                          # choose what goes into the snapshot
git commit -m "Add chapter 1"             # save it

echo "A dragon appears." >> book.txt
git commit -am "Add a paragraph about dragons"

git switch -c kill-character              # a new branch
echo "The knight dies." >> book.txt
git commit -am "Kill the knight in chapter 5"

git switch main                           # back to the main timeline
git merge kill-character                  # bring the branch in
git log --oneline
87cfb6f Kill the knight in chapter 5
7d36f0c Add a paragraph about dragons
d230ff8 Add chapter 1

Each line is one save point with its note. The branch name main may be master in older repositories.

What is it used for?

Developers use Git for code, but it works for anything made of text files:

  • writing a novel, a thesis or a report (including LaTeX and Quarto documents)
  • a collection of notes, such as an Obsidian vault
  • configuration files
  • a website like this blog

Git is less helpful for large binary files such as videos or Word documents, because it cannot show or merge their changes line by line.

Note

Git and GitHub are different things. Git is the tool that tracks history on our computer. GitHub is a website that stores repositories online and adds collaboration features.

Summary

Git takes a folder and gives it a searchable memory. Commits are save points, branches let us experiment safely, and merges bring the results together. Because we can always go back, we can try things without fear, and teams can work on one project at the same time without chaos.

item.title: Are C Pointers Unreliable When Array Addresses Change Between Runs?
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Take this loop, which prints the address of every element of an array:

int myNumbers[4] = {25, 50, 75, 100};
int i;

for (i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
  printf("%p\n", &myNumbers[i]);
}

Will it always print the same output? Can the addresses change with the operating system or the device? And if they do change, how can pointers be reliable at all? Let’s answer both questions.

Short answer

The spacing between the addresses is always the same. The actual numbers almost always change.

Within one run, we see something like:

0x7ffd4a3c2b40
0x7ffd4a3c2b44
0x7ffd4a3c2b48
0x7ffd4a3c2b4c

Each address is exactly 4 bytes after the previous one, because sizeof(int) is 4 here. C guarantees that array elements are contiguous. The starting address, however, will differ almost every time we run the program.

What is guaranteed and what changes

Property Guaranteed? Why
&myNumbers[i+1] - &myNumbers[i] == 1 ✅ Always Pointer arithmetic on int * counts elements
Neighbours are sizeof(int) bytes apart ✅ Always Arrays are contiguous in memory
The absolute value such as 0x7ffd... ❌ Almost never Depends on the OS, ASLR and the stack state
Same address across runs ❌ No ASLR randomizes the stack each run
Same address on a different device ❌ No Different OS, architecture and stack layout

Why the starting address changes

ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) is a security feature of modern operating systems. Each time a program starts, the OS places the stack at a random base address, so a local array such as myNumbers lands in a different spot. Running the same binary three times can give:

Run 1: 0x7ffd4a3c2b40
Run 2: 0x7ffc81e9d5a0
Run 3: 0x7ffd9f27c3e0

This makes it harder for attackers to predict where things live. The offset pattern (+0, +4, +8, +12) never changes; only the base moves.

Other things can shift the address too:

  • OS and compiler: stack alignment, the main prologue and variable ordering differ.
  • Architecture: a 32-bit build prints 8 hex digits, a 64-bit build prints up to 12 or more.
  • Compiler flags: -O0 and -O2 may reorder local variables.
  • Other variables: adding another local variable shifts the neighbours.

See it yourself

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int a[4] = {25, 50, 75, 100};
    int *p = a;                              // p holds the CURRENT address

    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)
        printf("%p\n", (void *)&a[i]);

    printf("gap    : %td bytes\n", (char *)&a[1] - (char *)&a[0]);
    printf("value  : %d\n", *p);
    printf("value  : %d\n", *(p + 2));

    int *q = &a[3];
    printf("offset : %td\n", q - p);
    return 0;
}

One run on Linux gave:

0x7ffd710965e0
0x7ffd710965e4
0x7ffd710965e8
0x7ffd710965ec
gap    : 4 bytes
value  : 25
value  : 75
offset : 3

Run it a few times: the four addresses change, while gap, value and offset stay identical.

To switch ASLR off for one run on Linux:

setarch $(uname -m) -R ./a.out

Now the same address prints every time, which shows the shifting was ASLR and not our code.

Note

%p expects a void *, so the strictly correct call is printf("%p\n", (void *)&a[i]);. Most compilers accept the version without the cast, but the cast is proper C. Likewise, print sizeof values with %zu.

So how can pointers be reliable?

A pointer stores the address as it is right now, not a fixed number. The address of an object is decided when the program runs, and then it does not change for the lifetime of that object:

  • ASLR picks the base address at startup.
  • &a[0] evaluates to whatever that base turned out to be.
  • The pointer stores that value.
  • *p reads from that exact address, which is where the array really is.

The pointer and the object always agree, because the pointer was computed from the object at runtime. Reliability comes not from the number being constant, but from the pointer and the object sharing the same current address.

Analogy: we don’t need to know a friend’s address in advance. We ask “where do you live?” and get the current one. Hardcoding an old address and hoping nobody moved is what fails.

Question Answer
Does &a[0] change while the program runs? ❌ No, an object’s address is fixed for its lifetime
Does p = &a[0]; *p read the right value? ✅ Always, within that run
Is &a[3] - &a[0] always 3? ✅ Always, offsets are stable even if the base moves
Does the number 0x7ffd... survive to the next run? ❌ No, ASLR changes it

What really makes pointers unreliable

ASLR is not the danger. These are:

  1. Hardcoding addresses: int *p = (int *)0x7ffd4a3c2b40; breaks on the next run.
  2. Dangling pointers: using a pointer after the object is freed, or after the function that owned a local variable returned.
  3. Saving pointers to disk or sending them to another process: the address means nothing there.
  4. Out-of-bounds arithmetic: a[10] on a four-element array points somewhere valid-looking but wrong.
  5. Comparing addresses across runs: the numbers differ, so == fails.

None of these involves ASLR itself. They all use a pointer outside the object’s valid lifetime, or treat an address as portable when it is not.

Why pointers are still the right tool

  • Computed, not memorized. &x asks the system where x is, and the answer is always current.
  • Type-aware. int *p tells the compiler to read 4 bytes as an int, whatever the numeric address.
  • Relative math is stable. p + 1 means the next int, that is address + sizeof(int), independent of the base.

Conclusion

Array addresses change between runs, devices and builds, because ASLR and the platform choose where the stack goes. What never changes is the layout: elements are contiguous and sizeof(T) apart, and a pointer always holds the actual current address of its object. So:

Never rely on a specific address value; rely on the relationships. Take the address with &, use it while the object is alive, and it is always correct. The address only looks unpredictable between runs, which is exactly when we should not be reusing the old number.

item.title: What void Means in C: Return Type vs. Parameter List
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Consider this function:

int myFunction(int x) {
  return 5 + x;
}

It takes an argument and returns a value, so replacing either part with void would break it. void is for the other kinds of functions, and it means something different depending on where we write it.

The four combinations

int  myFunction(int x)   // takes an int, returns an int
int  myFunction(void)    // takes nothing, returns an int
void myFunction(int x)   // takes an int, returns nothing
void myFunction(void)    // takes nothing, returns nothing

Case 1: void as the return type

The function has no result. Its whole job is a side effect, such as printing, writing to a file, or changing an array in place.

void greet(int times) {
    for (int i = 0; i < times; i++)
        printf("Hello\n");
}

We call it as a statement. Nothing comes back, so there is nothing to pass to printf:

greet(3);                 // correct
printf("%d", greet(3));   // error: invalid use of void expression

A sorting function is a typical example:

void bubbleSort(int a[], int n);   // sorts a[] in place, returns nothing

The array is changed through the pointer, so no return value is needed. Writing void documents that, and the compiler stops us from using a result that does not exist.

Case 2: void as the parameter list

int fortyTwo(void) {
    return 42;
}

Why not simply write int fortyTwo()? In C (before C23), empty parentheses mean unspecified arguments, which is the old pre-prototype style. The compiler does not check calls against it. The test below compiles without a single error:

int f();                       // unspecified parameters
int main(void) { return f(1, 2, 3); }   // accepted

With (void) the compiler enforces zero arguments:

int f(void) { return 7; }
int main(void) { return f(1); }
error: too many arguments to function ‘f’

So int f(void) gives us type checking, which is the main reason to write it in C. In C++, and from C23 onward, f() and f(void) mean the same thing, but writing (void) is still correct and works with older compilers.

What void does to myFunction

Change Effect
void myFunction(int x) printf("%d", myFunction(3)) no longer compiles. Call it as myFunction(3); instead.
int myFunction(void) myFunction(3) is an error, since it now takes no arguments.
void myFunction(void) Both the call and the printf break.

Our function needs an input and produces an output, so void is the wrong tool for it.

All together

#include <stdio.h>

int  add(int a, int b)  { return a + b; }          // returns a value
void show(int n)        { printf("%d\n", n); }     // side effect only
int  fortyTwo(void)     { return 42; }             // takes nothing

int main(void) {
    printf("%d\n", add(2, 3));   // value used
    show(add(2, 3));             // value passed to a void function
    printf("%d\n", fortyTwo());  // called with no arguments
    return 0;
}
5
5
42

show “just prints”, fortyTwo “takes nothing”, and main(void) “takes no command-line arguments”.

Tip

The rule. A void return means “call me for what I do, not for a value”. A void parameter list means “I take no arguments, and the compiler should enforce that”. If a function needs to take or give a value, use neither.

item.title: git add -A, git add . or git add *: Which One?
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Three commands look similar, but they do not stage the same things:

git add -A
git add .
git add *

The short answer: use git add -A or git add ., and avoid git add *. Let’s see why.

A test repository

We made a small repository with a .gitignore that lists node_modules/, committed it, and then changed things:

  • modified a.txt,
  • deleted b.txt,
  • created new.txt, sub/new2.txt and the hidden file .hidden,
  • created an ignored file node_modules/m2.js.

The results below are from git 2.34.

git add -A: everything in the repository

It stages new, modified and deleted files across the whole repository, whatever directory we run it from, and it respects .gitignore.

$ cd sub && git add -A && git status --short
A  .hidden
M  a.txt
D  b.txt
A  new.txt
A  sub/new2.txt

git add .: everything from here down

Since Git 2.0 it also stages deletions, but only in the current directory and below. From the repository root it does the same as git add -A. From a subfolder it does not:

$ cd sub && git add . && git status --short
 M a.txt
 D b.txt
A  sub/new2.txt
?? .hidden
?? new.txt

Only sub/new2.txt was staged. The changes outside sub/ were left alone.

git add *: a shell wildcard, not a Git feature

The shell expands * into a list of file names before Git runs, so Git never sees the pattern. That causes three problems:

  1. Hidden files are skipped. * does not match names that start with a dot, such as .hidden, .env or .github.
  2. Deletions are missed. A deleted file no longer exists, so * cannot expand to it.
  3. Ignored folders cause an error. If node_modules is in the current directory, * hands it to Git, which refuses:
$ git add *
The following paths are ignored by one of your .gitignore files:
node_modules
hint: Use -f if you really want to add them.

Git exits with an error, yet it still staged the other files:

M  a.txt
 D b.txt
A  new.txt
A  sub/new2.txt
?? .hidden

a.txt, new.txt and sub/new2.txt are staged, but b.txt (deleted) and .hidden are not. That mix of staged and missed changes is easy to commit by accident.

Which one should we use?

Command Scope New Modified Deleted Hidden
git add -A whole repository yes yes yes yes
git add . current folder and below yes yes yes yes
git add * non-hidden names in the current folder yes yes no no
  • At the repository root, git add . and git add -A are the same, so either is fine.
  • In a subfolder, choose by intent: git add . for this folder only, git add -A for everything.
  • Skip git add *.
Warning

Before staging, run git status, and check the result with git status or git diff --staged afterwards. Files such as .env secrets, build folders and temporary files should be in .gitignore first, because git add -A and git add . will stage anything that is not ignored.

item.title: Line Breaks in LaTeX: Which Command to Use
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
In LaTeX, pressing Enter once does nothing: a single newline in the source is treated as a space. To start a new line we need a command. Which one depends on what we want the text around the break to look like.

\\ and \newline: break now, leave the line short

First line\\
Second line

Both commands end the current line at once and continue on the next line, without starting a new paragraph. The line is not stretched, so it ends early and leaves an empty space at the right.

Two useful variants of \\:

  • \\[2ex] adds extra vertical space after the break.
  • \\* also forbids a page break right after the line.
Title\\[2ex]
Text that starts a little lower.

\linebreak: break now, stretch the line

This text is broken here\linebreak and the rest continues on the next line.

\linebreak also ends the line at that spot, but it stretches the spaces so the line reaches the right margin. With only a few words on the line, the gaps become large and ugly:

This       text      is     broken      here
and the rest continues on the next line.

It takes an optional strength from 0 to 4, written \linebreak[n]. A value of 4, the default, forces the break. Smaller values only request one, which LaTeX may ignore.

A new paragraph: blank line or \par

End of the first paragraph.

Start of the second paragraph.

A blank line in the source (or the \par command) ends the paragraph. Depending on the document class, the next paragraph gets an indent or extra vertical space. If we only want the next line, not a new paragraph, we should not use a blank line.

Inside tables

In a tabular, \\ ends the row, not just the line:

\begin{tabular}{ll}
  a\\b & c \\
  d & e
\end{tabular}

This gives three rows: a, then b c, then d e. To break a line inside one cell, the column must be a paragraph column such as p{3cm}, and we use \newline:

\begin{tabular}{p{3cm}l}
  first\newline second & x \\
\end{tabular}
first    x
second

In an ordinary l, c or r column, \newline has no effect, and the cell stays on one line.

Comparison

Command Effect Right margin
\\, \newline Ends the line at once Line stays short
\\* Ends the line at once, no page break after it Line stays short
\\[2ex] Ends the line, adds vertical space Line stays short
\linebreak Ends the line at once Line is stretched
blank line, \par Ends the paragraph Last line stays short
Tip

For spacing between lines or paragraphs, avoid stacking \\ commands. Use \\[length], or set \parskip and \parindent once in the preamble, so the layout stays consistent.

item.title: Create Multiple Files at Once in the Linux Terminal
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Creating files one by one in a file manager is slow. In the terminal, a single touch command can create as many as we like. It works the same way in Linux and macOS shells such as bash and zsh.

touch creates an empty file if it does not exist. If the file already exists, it only updates the modification time and leaves the contents alone.

1. Files with different names

When the names have nothing in common, we list them separated by spaces:

touch index.html styles.css script.js

2. Numbered or lettered files (brace expansion)

A range inside curly braces, {start..end}, is expanded by the shell before touch runs, so one pattern becomes many names:

# file1.txt, file2.txt, ..., file5.txt
touch file{1..5}.txt

# log_A.txt, log_B.txt, ..., log_E.txt
touch log_{A..E}.txt

To pad the numbers with zeros, write the first number with the zeros:

# bspl0001.c, bspl0002.c, bspl0003.c
touch bspl{0001..0003}.c

To preview what a pattern expands to without creating anything, use echo:

echo file{1..5}.txt
file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt file4.txt file5.txt

3. A chosen set of names

For specific names that share a prefix or extension, list the variations separated by commas. There must be no spaces inside the braces:

# test.js, demo.js, final.js
touch {test,demo,final}.js

4. Files inside a folder

Brace expansion also works after a path, so we can create files somewhere else without changing the current directory. The folder must already exist:

mkdir my_folder
touch my_folder/{file1.txt,file2.txt,file3.txt}

To create the folders at the same time, mkdir -p accepts braces too:

mkdir -p proj/{src,docs}
touch proj/src/{main,util}.c proj/docs/readme.md
ls -R proj
proj:
docs  src

proj/docs:
readme.md

proj/src:
main.c  util.c

5. Files with some starting text

touch always makes empty files. If each file needs a line of text, a short loop does it:

for i in 1 2 3; do echo "This is note $i" > note$i.txt; done
Note

Brace expansion is a feature of the shell, not of touch, so it works with any command (mkdir, cp, rm). The {1..5} range form needs bash or zsh: fish and a plain sh leave file{1..3}.txt unexpanded. All the examples above were run in bash.

item.title: Convert PowerPoint (PPT, PPTX) to PDF from the Command Line, in Bulk
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Opening each presentation and choosing Export as PDF is fine for one file and painful for fifty. The terminal can do it for us. The simplest tool is LibreOffice running without a window; the rest of this post covers a few alternatives.

LibreOffice (Linux, macOS, Windows)

LibreOffice is installed on many Linux distributions already, and its --headless mode converts files without opening the GUI.

Convert a single file:

libreoffice --headless --convert-to pdf presentation.pptx

Convert every .pptx in the current folder:

libreoffice --headless --convert-to pdf *.pptx

The PDFs are written to the current directory. To put them somewhere else, add --outdir:

libreoffice --headless --convert-to pdf --outdir pdf/ *.pptx

Old .ppt files work the same way; use *.ppt instead.

A whole folder tree

The glob *.pptx only sees one folder. To convert files in sub-folders too, let find feed them in, keeping each PDF next to its source:

find . -type f \( -iname '*.pptx' -o -iname '*.ppt' \) -print0 |
  while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    libreoffice --headless --convert-to pdf --outdir "$(dirname "$f")" "$f"
  done

-print0 with read -d '' keeps file names that contain spaces intact.

Note

If LibreOffice is already open in the GUI, a headless run may do nothing. Close the window first. On macOS the executable is usually /Applications/LibreOffice.app/Contents/MacOS/soffice, and on Linux soffice is the same program as libreoffice.

unoconv (Linux)

unoconv is a command-line wrapper around LibreOffice.

sudo apt-get install unoconv
unoconv -f pdf presentation.ppt

It needs LibreOffice installed too, so for a plain conversion the direct command above is simpler.

Win2PDF (Windows)

On Windows with Win2PDF Pro, the win2pdfd.exe utility converts from the command line:

win2pdfd.exe ppt2pdf "source.ppt" "dest.pdf"
win2pdfd.exe pptx2pdf "source.pptx" "dest.pdf"

This is a commercial product; see the Win2PDF documentation for the details.

ONLYOFFICE Document Builder

Unlike LibreOffice, ONLYOFFICE has no single conversion flag. Its Document Builder (Windows, Linux, macOS) runs a small JavaScript file. Save this as convert.js:

builder.OpenFile("presentation.pptx");
builder.SaveFile("pdf", "presentation.pdf");
builder.CloseFile();

and run it:

documentbuilder convert.js      # Linux and macOS
docbuilder.exe convert.js       # Windows

There is no built-in recursive mode. To convert a folder tree, wrap the call in a Bash or PowerShell loop that generates the script (or passes the paths) for each file. If we run a self-hosted ONLYOFFICE Document Server, its Conversion API can do the same job through an HTTP POST with curl.

Which one to use

Need Tool
One file or one folder libreoffice --headless --convert-to pdf
Many folders the find loop above
Windows with Win2PDF Pro win2pdfd.exe
Already using ONLYOFFICE Document Builder or the Conversion API

For most of us, headless LibreOffice is enough: one command, no scripting. Check a converted PDF or two, since fonts missing on the machine are replaced and can change the layout.

References

  • Ask Ubuntu: How can I convert a PPT to a PDF from the command line?
  • Win2PDF: command-line PPT to PDF and PPTX to PDF
  • ONLYOFFICE Document Builder: using the CLI

item.title: Printing Array Elements in C: Labels, Commas, and Clean Output
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
We have an array and want one tidy line of output:

The printed values of the array: 2, 5, 7, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 23, 25

Our first attempt puts the whole message inside the loop:

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int FixedArr[10] = {2, 5, 7, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 23, 25};

    for (int val = 0; val < 10; val++) {
        printf("The printed values of the array: %d, ", FixedArr[val]);
    }
    return 0;
}

Output:

The printed values of the array: 2, The printed values of the array: 5, The printed values of the array: 7, ...

(Every program in this post was compiled with gcc -Wall -Wextra and run; the outputs are real.)

Why the label repeats

The body of a loop runs once per element, and printf prints its whole format string every time. The label is part of that string, so it is printed ten times. We want it once.

Anything that should appear once goes outside the loop. The loop body should print only what repeats for each element.
